lexical.adversarial_notes:
Searched the following queries: (1) 'national blackout November 17 2026', (2) 'blackout November 17 2026 power grid', (3) 'November 17 2026 blackout rumor origin earliest TikTok post October'. No pre-2026-09-16 instances of the 'national blackout November 17 2026' narrative framing were found.

Key findings that support the proposed earliest date of 2026-09-16 as the logical origin anchor:

(a) The FCC published its public notice (DA 26-989) scheduling the nationwide EAS test for November 17, 2026 on September 16, 2026 — this is the real-world event that gave the framing its specific date. Multiple sources (preparedstates.com, sherafy.com) explicitly cite 'Sep 16, 2026' as the date of the FEMA/FCC press release and FCC public notice. The framing could not logically have named November 17 as a blackout date before that announcement existed.

(b) The earliest documented social-media instance of the blackout rumor itself is October 27, 2026, per EFE's reporting as cited by sherafy.com: 'EFE later identifies an English-language social-media post predicting a November 17 blackout' on that date, described explicitly as 'an early traceable instance, not proof of the rumor's first origin.' PolitiFact's source list cites the earliest TikTok post it reviewed as November 2, 2026.

(c) No Usenet archives, Google Books results, newspaper archives, congressional records, or pre-September 2026 blog/forum posts were returned containing the specific framing 'national blackout November 17 2026,' 'grid failure November 17,' 'blackout November 17 2026,' or 'nationwide blackout coming November 17.' All results were from November 2026 (fact-checks, news articles) or were entirely unrelated real blackout events (Cuba, Dominican Republic, Berlin, Ukraine).

(d) Near-misses considered and ruled out: The Simpsons episode ('It's a Blunderful Life') was noted by multiple fact-checkers as depicting a fictional Springfield blackout with a November 17 date in Lisa's diary. This is fiction depicting the claim's content, not an assertion of it — ruled out per the FICTION IS NOT ATTESTATION rule; it is at most related context. The Pentagon's FORTRESS America 90-day grid-independence initiative was also cited as a contributing amplifier but does not itself assert a November 17 blackout date.

(e) Limitations: TikTok's own archive is not publicly searchable; early deleted posts from October 2026 may exist but are not recoverable via web search. Paywalled social-media analytics tools (e.g., Brandwatch, Meltwater) that might surface the very first post were not accessible. The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine was not directly queried (no remaining search calls), but all indexed web sources returned were post-September 16, 2026. The proposed date of 2026-09-16 appears well-supported as the earliest possible anchor for this framing, since the specific date 'November 17' could not have been named in this context before the FEMA/FCC announcement that day.

conceptual.adversarial_notes:
The structural claim under examination is: 'a widespread electrical grid failure will occur on a specific date,' with a causal agent triggering a cascading nationwide blackout. The proposed anchor date is 1965-11-09 — the date of the actual Northeast Blackout, not a prediction of it. This is a critical disambiguation: the 1965-11-09 event is the OCCURRENCE of the blackout, not a prior prediction that it would occur on that date. The structural claim as stated is therefore the event itself, not a prophecy or forecast. This significantly constrains what could count as an 'earlier articulation': it would require a pre-1965-11-09 text asserting that a specific date would bring a widespread US grid failure.

Traditions and sources checked:

1. PRE-1965 FEDERAL REGULATORY WARNINGS: The Federal Power Commission (FPC) was actively urging utilities to form larger regional grids before 1965, and in 1964 recommended reducing generating reserve capacity. However, these were general reliability policy recommendations, not date-specific predictions of a blackout. They are related-context (doctrine), not earlier articulations of the same structural claim form.

2. ENGINEERING AND ACADEMIC LITERATURE PRE-1965: The concept of cascading failure in interconnected power systems was understood by electrical engineers before 1965 — the interconnected CANUSE grid was itself a known design with known interdependencies. However, no pre-1965 engineering paper or report asserting that a specific date would bring a nationwide blackout was found. General vulnerability analysis is doctrine, not the same structural claim.

3. CIVIL DEFENSE / WARTIME BLACKOUT PREDICTIONS: WWII-era civil defense blackouts (1941–1945) were deliberate, scheduled, and localized — not predictions of uncontrolled cascading grid failure. These are a different structural form entirely (deliberate drill vs. uncontrolled failure).

4. FICTION AND SPECULATIVE LITERATURE: Per the FICTION IS NOT ATTESTATION rule, any pre-1965 science fiction or thriller depicting a grid failure on a specific date would not qualify as an earlier articulation. No such fiction was found in searches that would even tempt this classification.

5. CONSPIRACY / PROPHECY TRADITIONS: No pre-1965 prophetic or conspiratorial text predicting a specific-date US grid blackout was found. The closest contemporary analog found is a November 2026 viral hoax predicting a November 17, 2026 worldwide blackout — a structurally identical claim form, but it post-dates the anchor by 61 years and is therefore irrelevant to the adversarial search.

6. REFERENT-BOUND CONSTRAINT: The 1965-11-09 Northeast Blackout is a named, dated event. Nothing predating the event's existence can be an earlier articulation of a claim about that specific event occurring on that specific date. The event had no known public predictor who named November 9, 1965 in advance. The FPC's 1964 reserve-capacity recommendation is the closest pre-event institutional document, but it is general policy doctrine, not a date-specific failure prediction.

CONCLUSION: The search yields a clean negative result. No earlier text — engineering, regulatory, prophetic, fictional, or conspiratorial — has been found that articulates the same structural claim: that a widespread US electrical grid failure would occur on a specific named date. The 1965-11-09 event is, by the historical record, the first instance of this structural claim being 'realized,' and no prior articulation of it as a prediction has been identified. This clean negative strengthens the proposed anchor date as the earliest known instantiation of the claim's realization, while also confirming that the claim form (date-specific grid failure prediction) has no documented pre-1965 ancestor in the English-language US tradition.

sources.title: FEMA/FCC Official Press Release: 2026 Nationwide EAS Test Scheduled for November 17
sources.description: FEMA and the FCC officially announced a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System (EAS) for November 17, 2026 at approximately 2:20 p.m. ET, with a backup date of December 3, 2026. The test interrupts radio and TV programming only; no mobile alerts, no power disruption.
sources.notes: The single real, scheduled federal event on November 17, 2026 — a routine EAS test, not a power outage — is the factual anchor that viral blackout claims have been grafted onto.

sources.title: FEMA FAQ: 2026 National EAS Test
sources.description: FEMA's official FAQ clarifies that the EAS test is required by the IPAWS Modernization Act of 2015 at least once every three years, lasts about one minute on TV and radio, and explicitly states no public action is required.
sources.notes: Directly addresses the legal basis and scope of the November 17 test, confirming it has no connection to any power grid shutdown.

sources.title: PolitiFact / WBAL Fact-Check: 'No evidence that a US blackout is expected Nov. 17'
sources.description: A PolitiFact fact-check, syndicated by WBAL and KOCO, rates the claim that a 90-day nationwide blackout will begin November 17, 2026 as false. It notes that a video purportedly showing Trump announcing a blackout was manipulated, and that no federal announcement of any grid shutdown has been made.
sources.notes: Directly disputes the claim; cites DHS Secretary statement and absence of any federal announcement; flags manipulated video as a key vector of misinformation.

sources.title: Snopes: 'Is 90-day blackout beginning Nov. 17? Why unfounded rumor is spreading'
sources.description: Snopes investigates the viral claim and finds no evidence that a 90-day blackout will follow the EAS test. It identifies the claim's origins in social media posts and the Simpsons episode, and notes the episode's plot does not match the 2026 calendar.
sources.notes: Comprehensive debunk covering all major vectors of the claim — government conspiracy, cyberattack, and Simpsons 'prediction' — finding no supporting evidence for any.

sources.title: AOL / USA Today Network: 'Is 90-day blackout happening Nov. 17 in Florida?'
sources.description: Reports that no federal announcement of a nationwide 90-day blackout or plans to shut down the US power grid on November 17 have been made, and that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no need to stockpile supplies.
sources.notes: Adds an on-record government denial from DHS Secretary, strengthening the dispute; also contextualizes the role of recent tech outages in stoking speculation.

sources.title: The Simpsons, 'It's a Blunderful Life' (Season 35, Episode 7)
sources.description: The 2023 Thanksgiving episode of The Simpsons features a fictional Springfield blackout beginning on November 17. Lisa's diary references that date. The episode never specifies a year, the blackout is local to Springfield (not national or global), and the episode's internal calendar (Thanksgiving six days later) matches 2023, not 2026.
sources.notes: The real episode is the primary cultural artifact driving the viral claim; its actual content (no year, no national scope, calendar mismatch with 2026) directly undermines the 'prediction' interpretation.

sources.title: PreparedStates.com: 'November 17 Blackout? What's Really Scheduled, Checked'
sources.description: An independent preparedness site verifies what is actually scheduled on November 17 (a one-minute EAS test on TV and radio) and notes that the viral claim that the Simpsons episode names November 17 in its final seconds has not been independently verified, and that the viral video splices in scenes from another episode.
sources.notes: Redirects from the blackout claim to the verifiable scheduled event; raises the additional point that the viral video itself may be manipulated, not just misinterpreted.

sources.title: TikTok viral posts (multiple accounts, Nov. 2–14, 2026)
sources.description: Multiple TikTok posts beginning around November 1–2, 2026 claimed a 90-day nationwide blackout would begin November 17, citing the Simpsons episode and a manipulated video of Trump. These posts are the primary origin and amplification mechanism of the claim.
sources.notes: The only 'supporting' evidence for the claim is social media posts; no primary source, official document, or technical analysis underpins the prediction.

sources.title: IEEE-USA Position Statement: Cybersecurity and the Electrical Power Grid (Feb. 2026)
sources.description: IEEE-USA's board formally stated that US electric power systems are under 'persistent, escalating cyberattacks' and that new security measures are insufficient to reverse increased vulnerability to coordinated attacks by hostile state actors. A cyberattack on the grid poses severe risk of cascading failures across sectors.

sources.title: Breezyscroll Fact-Check: 'The Simpsons Blackout Clip Is Real. The November 17 Prediction Isn't'

evidence_landscape.summary: The claim of a national blackout on November 17, 2026 is a viral social media rumor with no supporting primary evidence. It originated from TikTok posts in early November 2026 that fused two real but unrelated events — a routine FEMA/FCC Emergency Alert System test scheduled for that date, and a 2023 Simpsons episode featuring a fictional Springfield blackout referencing November 17 — into a fabricated prediction, amplified by a manipulated video falsely attributed to Trump. Every major fact-checking outlet (PolitiFact, Snopes, AOL/USA Today) and official government source (FEMA, FCC, DHS) has directly disputed the claim. The genuine shared context is that the US grid does face documented, serious structural vulnerabilities — aging infrastructure, cybersecurity threats, cascading failure risk, and geomagnetic storm exposure near solar maximum — but none of these factors point to a specific date, and no technical or official source has identified November 17, 2026 as a date of elevated risk.
